attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post. He endorses them.

semantics.note: 'Highly doubt' is high confidence that AGI will not arrive within three years, so it is a scored directional forecast. The ten-year clause is kept as an uncertainty statement, not as a second forecast.

contract.note: Reading three years as ending 2028-05-22 and AGI as broad human-level capability is an ordinary reading. Requiring independent verification rather than company claims or one benchmark is fair.

evidence.note: A Sept 2026 review that says no accepted AGI test exists and that the claims it reviewed do not establish AGI. It is relevant to the early-resolution check but cannot settle a deadline that is still ahead.
ARC Prize reports strong ARC-AGI-3 results for Astra but explicitly says it is not claiming AGI. This does not meet the early-resolution rule.

reviews.rationale: The deadline is 2028-05-22, after the evaluation date. No dated, independently verified demonstration of broad AGI appears in the packet, and ARC Prize itself disclaims AGI for Astra. The early-resolution rule is not met, so the forecast cannot be scored yet.

contract.note: Using the scenario's 2027 milestones as the comparison point is fair. However, support requires an established AGI arrival date, which would leave the claim unscorable if AGI never arrives. It is also labelled retrospective although it is a forecast.

evidence.note: The AI 2027 scenario text establishes the comparison milestones (e.g. a superhuman AI researcher in Sept 2027). It is not evidence of what actually happened.
A May 2026 preprint saying there is no clear framework for measuring progress toward AGI. It is about measurement, not about whether AGI has arrived.

reviews.rationale: No terminal deadline was stated, and the scenario's 2027 comparison point has not yet arrived. The packet contains no independently established arrival of general intelligence that would trigger early contradiction. The outcome cannot be settled at the evaluation date.

semantics.note: The normalisation matches the sentence. It is a causal or rhetorical objection to the scenario's mechanism, with no measure, rate or horizon.

contract.note: The contract rightly declines to supply a metric or extrapolation model the speaker did not give. Treating the claim as not adjudicable is fair.

evidence.note: The METR paper reports time horizons doubling about every 7 months. It is a progress trend and does not test whether 'tiny' daily gains can produce the scenario's leaps.

reviews.rationale: The claim names no measure of daily gains, no definition of the 'quantum leaps', and no way to separate incremental gains from other causes. Any binary test would invent specifics the speaker did not supply, so the claim cannot be scored.

semantics.note: Adding 'useful' and 'unverifiable' follows from the next sentence ('We can't verify data like that'). The scope is limited to many open-ended domains, such as geopolitical and economic counterfactuals.

contract.note: The plain reading (validated training data for open-ended counterfactual scenarios, not merely generating narratives) is fair and ordinary. 'Many' has no denominator, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: A Dec 2024 preprint noting that forecasting ground truth only arrives later, and proposing consistency checks as stand-ins. It neither proves nor refutes the claim.
A 2024 self-supervised forecasting fine-tune trained on resolved historical questions. It does not validate synthetic answers for novel counterfactuals like the speaker's examples.
A Feb 2025 paper training on synthetic time-series data. This is a different, statistical task from open-ended geopolitical scenarios.

reviews.rationale: No item shows reliable, validated synthetic training data for open-ended geopolitical or economic counterfactuals, which the contradiction condition requires. Nor does any item directly establish that such methods were unavailable across many domains, which the support condition requires. The packet settles neither side.
